cards.title: F. G. Foster
cards.body: "Standard numbering in the book trade; a report by F. G. Foster." Publishers Association, London, 1967 — nine pages, twenty centimetres, catalogued at the Library of Congress as LCCN 79398313, shelfmark Z323 .F6. Its subject heading reads "Publishers' standard book numbers — Standards — Great Britain": a national trade problem, not a plan for a global identifier.
cards.prompt: W. H. Smith was moving to a computerised warehouse and the British trade wanted one number per book. In 1967 the Publishers Association published a nine-page report on standard numbering — who wrote it, and where?
cards.answer: F. G. Foster. The Publishers Association published it in London in 1967: nine pages, twenty centimetres, Library of Congress LCCN 79398313.

cards.title: The ten-digit space runs dry
cards.body: ISO: "the very success of the ISBN system, up to now based on 10 digits, has been causing it to run out of capacity." Every system that recorded, stored or exchanged ISBN data had to accept thirteen digits by 1 January 2007. The standard that obliged them listed at 99 Swiss francs.
cards.prompt: The ISBN did not change length because anyone wanted a nicer number. What did ISO say had gone wrong, and what single deadline did it hand the entire book trade?
cards.answer: The 10-digit system was running out of capacity, so the 2005 fourth edition moved it to thirteen digits; every automated system in the trade had to be ready by one date, 1 January 2007.

cards.title: ISO 2108, clause 4.4
cards.body: Clause 4.4: "The registrant element varies in length according to the projected publication output of each publisher." Clause 4.6: the check digit uses a modulus 10 algorithm. Clause 5.4: once assigned, an ISBN "shall not be altered, replaced, or re-used." Three clauses, three of your design decisions.
cards.prompt: One clause of the ISBN standard is the one a shortener designer should read. Which element does it govern, and what does it say decides that element's width?
cards.answer: Clause 4.4, the registrant element — the publisher's block. Its length varies according to the projected publication output of each publisher, so the width is a forecast, fixed once at assignment.

cards.title: Why your ID generator leases blocks
cards.body: "Publishers with the largest expected title outputs are assigned the shortest registrant elements and vice versa." The agency is called once, at the block; after that the publisher numbers out of it with no network round trip, and comes back only when it is exhausted. Leasing a million IDs from a counter table is the same bargain.
cards.prompt: A publisher mints an ISBN without asking any central service for the next number. What was paid once to buy that, and which line of this chapter's design is the identical trade?
cards.answer: Coordination was paid once, at block assignment: the agency issues a registrant element sized to forecast output, then the publisher numbers locally until that block is exhausted. The same trade is leasing a block of a million IDs from the counter row and minting from local memory.
